messages.body_plain:
Hi Juliet:

I didn't notice that plot.likert() set the zero value at the center of
the 'no opinion' bar; thank you for noting that. It makes a certain
amount of sense visually, but I'm not thrilled with the scaling of the
x-axis for two reasons: (i) the horizontal scale doesn't define
positive and negative values, and (ii) it is certainly not
representing 'frequency' unambiguously. I think the central question
in this plot is: what does zero mean? Given that bar plots use zero as
an anchor point, I'm wondering if this is a suitable graphical
metaphor for the intended message of the graph. I don't have any
immediate answers, but it's worth pondering.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: ggplot figure tweaking/clipping
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Dennis. Yes, fig=TRUE is not necessary; knitr will always try to capture plots unless you set fig.keep=none (whereas in Sweave you have to tell it fig=TRUE). And pdf() + dev.off() should almost never appear in R code.

On Tuesday, January 31, 2012 11:34:58 AM UTC-6, Dennis Murphy wrote:

>
> Side note: knitr will save plots created within the document in the
> same directory where the .Rnw file resides. If you want saved 7 x 7
> plots, you should make fig.width and fig.height = 7 in the
> \SweaveOpts{} chunk. It's also worth naming the code chunks because
> the graphs will get saved with the name of the chunk. [chunk-name.dev <http://chunk-name.dev>,
> where dev is the device specified.] In addition, you don't need
> fig=TRUE in version 0.2; the argument has been deprecated and replaced
> by fig.show and fig.keep. See the most recent documentation at the
> knitr web site for details.

> Dennis
>

I think the problem is that you did nothing to set up a plot -
geom_hline() provides a form of annotation. This is roundabout but
seems to work:

    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = value)) + ylim(10.1, 10.2)

the values,  then inserted the two lines with geom_hline().

messages.subject: Re: Legend position challenges in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

If space is a premium, perhaps you could place the legends inside the
graphics region. You'll need to play around with the parameter values,
but try something like this:

ggplot() + ... + opts(legend.position = c(0.7, 0.2))

where the x and y values are proportions of the total graphics space
in each direction. You want to do this in the size of the plot you
intend to publish, because if you do it at the default size and shrink
later, the legends don't always scale the same way as the interior of
the graph.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Why doesn't stat_summary() work when x is a factor?
messages.subject_clean: Why doesn't stat_summary() work when x is a factor?
messages.body_plain:
On 1/23/2012 7:01 AM, David Cooper wrote:
> My question: Why does case 2 not behave like case 1?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Dave
>
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
>
> # case1:  stat_summary() connects the means when x is numeric:
> c<- qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)
> c + stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom='line')
>
> # case2:  but stat_summary() doesn' work when x is a factor.  why??
> c<- qplot(factor(cyl), mpg, data=mtcars)
> c + stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom='line')
>
> # case3:  However, this code with geom_line, works whether x is factor or
> numeric
> c<- qplot(factor(cyl), mpg, data=mtcars)
> # c<- qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)
> c + geom_line(aes(group=1), stat='summary', fun.y='mean')

You need the aes(group=1) to make it work across factors:

qplot(factor(cyl), mpg, data=mtcars) +
   stat_summary(aes(group=1), fun.y = mean, geom='line')

Also, don't use c as a variable name; too much chance of causing
problems with the c function.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: Conceptual confusion with geom_segment and aes regarding line color
messages.subject_clean: Conceptual confusion with geom_segment and aes regarding line color
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

aes() maps aesthetics (such as color) to variables. So aes(color = "black")
maps color to a variable who's values are all the same (i.e., "black").
compare to aes(color = "someFunkyTextString") -- you'll get the same thing,
except for the different label in the legend. Again, the reason is that you
are mapping color to this variable, not setting it to a fixed value. If you
want to set an aesthetic to a fixed value, do so outside of the aes() call.
Outside of aes() color = "black" sets the color to black.

Hope that helps,

Ista

have very different scales so I want to use free scales. I then want to

and the categorical variable on y in the first place because I want to
use geom_pointrange().  I'm using facet_grid() rather than facet_wrap()
because I want to suppress the y-axes on the all but the leftmost planel.

easier than e.g. repeating

messages.subject: Re: Simple geom_line plot question
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's a simple take on the problem. You're neither going to get tick
marks inside the plot region with ggplot2 nor get 'x 10^4' in the
upper left corner, though.

library('ggplot2')
# library('reshape2')    ## if using 0.9.0 devel
# Don't need a path if the data frame is the current R directory
# see getwd() and setwd()
d <- read.csv('/path/to/testwave_small12.csv', header = FALSE)

# Take the twelve series and melt (or equivalently, stack) them:
dm <- melt(d)
# add an index variable:
dm$index <- rep(1:32, 12)

# dm$variable is a factor with a level for each series; use it
# as a grouping variable. dm$value holds the values of each series.

# This produces a 'spaghetti plot' (familiar to mixed modelers):
ggplot(dm, aes(x = index, y = value/10000, group = variable)) + geom_line() +
    labs(x = "", y = expression('value'~phantom(1) %*% 10^4))

All the expression() silliness was to put in a multiplication operator
x; the phantom(1) part is to put a 'phantom value' 1 before the
operator since it is binary.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Art,

I took a slightly different approach from Dennis and Winston.  They
changed the data to get the different labels on the graph.  I
perosnally prefer to preserve the data and change the labels.  I also
show the black and white theme which is closer to your matlab example.
 If you really want the x 10 ^4 jazz at the top left, it could be done
with text placement, but it seems like a lot of work, for something
that confused me at first anyway.

Cheers,

Josh

dat <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = FALSE)
dat$x <- 1:nrow(dat)

require(reshape)
require(ggplot2)

longdat <- melt(dat, id.vars = "x")
## break points
b <- seq(-4, 4, 2)

## device with same ratio as yours
dev.new <http://dev.new>(height = 6, width = 8)

## base setting
ggplot(data = longdat, aes(x = x, y = value, group = variable)) +
  ## use lines for plot
  geom_line() +
  ## give the y axis a different name, and manually set the breaks and labels
  ## also the range
  scale_y_continuous(name = expression(x~10^4), limits = range(b) * 10^4,
    expand = c(0, 0), breaks = b * 10^4, labels = b) +
  ## set range of x
  scale_x_continuous(name = "", limits = c(0, 35), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  ## use a black and white theme instead of the grey background
  theme_bw()

messages.body_plain:
On 2/4/2012 8:33 AM, Ben Bolker wrote:
> On 12-02-04 11:28 AM, Brandon Hurr wrote:
>> The only solutions I can think of are:
>>   (1) write a geom_hpointrange() that takes xmin and xmax rather than
>> ymin and ymax and generates a horizontal segment through the points;
>>   (2) use geom_point() and geom_segment() separately to get the same effect.
>> or...
>> (3) use geom_point() and geom_errorbarh()
>> <http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_errorbarh.html>to get the same effect.
>
>    Thanks.  It looks like geom_errorbarh(..., height=0) will be slightly
> cleaner than geom_segment(aes(y=y,yend=y,...))
>
>    cheers
>      Ben

Horizontal point ranges have been implemented a few times. I had one in
the ggExtra package (which isn't available anymore).  That code was:

#' An interval represented by a horizontal line.
#'
#' @name geom_hlinerange
#' @seealso \code{\link{geom_linerange}}: vertical line range;
#'   \code{\link{geom_errorbar}}: error bars;
#'   \code{\link{geom_pointrange}}: range indicated by straight line, with
#'   point in the middle; \code{\link{geom_crossbar}}: hollow bar with
middle
#'   indicated by horizontal line; \code{\link{stat_summary}}: examples of
#'   these guys in use; \code{\link{geom_smooth}}: for continuous analog
#' @export
#' @examples
GeomHlinerange <- proto(Geom, {
   objname <- "hlinerange"

   default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
   default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour = "black", size=0.5,
linetype=1, alpha = 1)
   guide_geom <- function(.) "path"
   required_aes <- c("xmin", "xmax", "y")

   draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
     munched <- coordinates$transform(data, scales)
     ggname(.$my_name(), GeomSegment$draw(transform(data, yend=y,
x=xmin, xend=xmax), scales, coordinates, ...))
   }

   icon <- function(.) segmentsGrob(c(0.1, 0.2), c(0.3, 0.7), c(0.7,
0.95), c(0.3, 0.7))

})

#' An interval represented by a horizontal line, with a point in the middle.
#'
#' @name geom_hpointrange
#' @seealso
#'  \code{\link{geom_errorbar}} for error bars,
#'  \code{\link{geom_linerange}} for range indicated by straight line,
examples,
#'  \code{\link{geom_crossbar}} for hollow bar with middle indicated by
horizontal line,
#'  \code{\link{stat_summary}} for examples of these guys in use,
#'  \code{\link{geom_smooth}} for continuous analog"
#' @export
#' @examples
#' # See geom_linerange for examples
GeomHpointrange <- proto(Geom, {
   objname <- "hpointrange"

   icon <- function(.) {
     gTree(children=gList(
       segmentsGrob(c(0.1, 0.2), c(0.3, 0.7), c(0.7, 0.95), c(0.3, 0.7)),
       pointsGrob(c(0.4, 0.6), c(0.3, 0.7), pch=19, gp=gpar(col="black",
cex=0.5), default.units="npc")
     ))
   }

   default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
   default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour = "black", size=0.5,
linetype=1, shape=16, fill=NA, alpha = 1)
   guide_geom <- function(.) "pointrange"
   required_aes <- c("y", "x", "xmin", "xmax")

   draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
     if (is.null(data$y)) return(GeomHlinerange$draw(data, scales,
coordinates, ...))
     ggname(.$my_name(),gTree(children=gList(
       GeomHlinerange$draw(data, scales, coordinates, ...),
       GeomPoint$draw(transform(data, size = size * 4), scales,
coordinates, ...)
     )))
   }

   draw_legend <- function(., data, ...) {
     data <- aesdefaults(data, .$default_aes(), list(...))

     grobTree(
       GeomPath$draw_legend(data, ...),
       GeomPoint$draw_legend(transform(data, size = size * 4), ...)
     )
   }

})

geom_hlinerange <- GeomHlinerange$build_accessor()
geom_hpointrange <- GeomHpointrange$build_accessor()

In doing a quick google search, there also seems to be something very
similar (though named geom_linerangeh and geom_pointrangeh) in the
ggplothacks package on github
(https://github.com/dschulman/ggplothacks). I've not used it, so I can't
vouch for it.

>> coord_flip() seems to always break stuff.

Agreed.  I'd like to see transposed geoms (like the above) to eliminate
the need for coord_flip() entirely.  That would be much cleaner and
would avoid many of the flip-only problems.

>> On Sat, Feb 4, 2012 at 16:20, Ben Bolker<bbolker-Re5JQEe...@public.gmane.org
>> <mailto:bbolker-Re5JQEe...@public.gmane.org>>  wrote:

messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Feb-03, at 14:15 , Emperorfish wrote:
>
> I wonder if you can advise me if you have time.  I am trying to
> produce a bubble map of the uk using the worldhires map from the map
> package, ggplot2 and I cannot seem to find a method to fill the land
> in with a shade of green like I can normally in R.  Here is my code
> from which I have used your example of NZ.
>
> reg <- as.data.frame(map("worldHires", xlim = c(-6, 9), ylim =
> c(51,62), plot = FALSE)[c("x", "y")])
> (ukmap <- qplot(x, y, data=reg, geom="path"))
>
> And then I just add the points using geom_points layer…
> This is the code I would normally use in R  map("worldHires", xlim =
> c(-6, 9), ylim = c(51,62),fill=T, col='grey', add=T, plot=T), I tried
> this but with no luck.
> Is there a simple method as I rather like your plots of north America
> where the states are blacked out?

If you want a closed and colored polygon, use geom_polygon.

reg <- as.data.frame(map("world", xlim = c(-6, 9), ylim = c(51,62), plot = FALSE)[c("x", "y")])
# NB: I don't have a worldHires map here
(ukmap <- qplot(x, y, data=reg, geom="polygon"))

But this would likely still not work but that's a problem with the data: the polygons need to be identified and closed in the data also for this to work. Here is does not work because the UK main isle is actually several pieces, as can be seen this way:

library("maps")
reg <- as.data.frame(map("world", xlim = c(-6, 9), ylim = c(51,62), plot = FALSE)[c("x", "y")])
# NB: I don't have a worldHires map here
library("ggplot2")
(ukmap <- qplot(x, y, data=reg, geom="polygon"))
# detect the pieces separated by NAs
reg$piece <- cumsum(is.na <http://is.na>(reg$x))
(ukmap <- qplot(x, y, fill=factor(piece), data=reg, geom="polygon"))

Hi

There is no official way to do that.
Here is a workaround:

qplot(1:3, 1:3)

grid.remove(grid.get("axis.ticks", grep=T, global = TRUE)[[1]]$name)
grid.remove(grid.get("axis.ticks", grep=T, global = TRUE)[[2]]$name)

these lines remove the ticks separately.

The function for controlling each axis separately will appear in

messages.subject: Re: Change font of graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin:

If you're using LaTeX and inserting the graph in a document with that
font, then your best bet is probably to use the tikzDevice package.
This post: http://www.macfreek.nl/memory/Fonts_in_LaTeX  shows how to
load the font in question in both LaTeX and Xe(La)TeX. I haven't used
tikzDevice myself, but several folks on this list have and may be able
to post an example or two. The idea behind the tikzDevice package is
to render text in R graphs using the same font as the standard text in
a LaTeX document.

Another attractive option if you are inserting the graph in a document
is the knitr package, which is quickly becoming a viable alternative
to Sweave. knitr supports approximately 20 graphics devices, including
tikz; the primary knitr manual has an example that uses the tikz
graphics device, using the tikzDevice package in the background. See
http://yihui.name/knitr/demos and click the manual link toward the
bottom of the page to get started.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: removing tick from one axis
messages.body_plain:
In general, my idea is that:

1) positional guides can be specified like
guides(x = guide_axis(), y = guide_table(), colour = ..., fill = ...)

2) some p-guides are supported:
- axis: similar as current axis
- table: table
- range: here is a good example. an absolute value is meaningless.
only a relative distance is meaningful.

etc, etc. give me idea, please.

- each guide can have their own parameters
guide_axis(ticks = TRUE, labels = fun, grid = TRUE)

- table is more complicated, and it accepts data:
guide_table(data = df, style = ...)
where the data is a data.frame of x (or y), text1, text2, ...

the gird may be a element of axis, etc, or grid maybe a guide, so
positional guides can be combined.

guides(x = list(guide_axis(), guide_grid()))

but I think probably grid should be an element of a guide.

Any suggestions are welcome!!

thanks,

kohske

messages.subject: change tile height dynamically

Hi everyone,

i want to visualize some dichotomous patterns over time (e.g. 1001)
and their frequency. My plot looks good already:

rep(c(3, 6), each = 4), variable = rep(1:4, 2), value = sample(c(0,1),
8, replace = TRUE))

    ggplot(df, aes(variable, name, fill = value)) +
geom_tile(colour = "white")

I now want to map the frequency on tiles height:

    ggplot(df, aes(variable, name, fill = value)) +
geom_tile(colour = "white")

This seems to work, but since my Freqs are > 1, the categories seem to
overplot. I guess, one would need to change the breaks on the y-axis?
Could someone suggest how to do this dynamically?

Best, Felix

messages.subject: Re: Will the ggplot2 .9 release be backward compatible?
messages.subject_clean: Will the ggplot2 .9 release be backward compatible?
messages.body_plain:
Some will be ok, some will break.  Hadley and others have put a lot of effort into trying to make things not break, but in some cases it hasn't been possible to make everything work.  That's also why the package will be released March 1 as opposed to the previous date - packages started breaking so the CRAN maintainers pulled it.

The changes are typically minor and have to do with things like legends. I would expect whatever code you have to still work as usual.

Cheers
david.

messages.subject: faceting a map
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I am fairly new to ggplot2 and am trying to work through some more advanced mapping features (I geocoded data and plotted it onto a map for the first time this week).  One thing I'd like to be able to do for visualization is faceting with the facet_grid argument.  I tried this and failed miserably.  I thought I'd go find some help on it but I can't even find a google image of it.  Is this possible?

Often hotmail or ,perhaps user malfunction, has a proclivity towards poorly formatted messages so I provided the code in a pastebin link as well.

##################################################
p <- ggplot()
p <- p + geom_polygon( data=states, aes(x=long, y=lat, group = group),
         colour="white" )
p <- p + geom_point(data=mydata, hjust=0.5, vjust=-0.5, aes(x=long, y=lat,
         label=label), colour="gold2", size=4 )
p  + facet_grid(liberal_arts~.)# massive fail angry message
#Error: Casting formula contains variables not found in molten data: liberal_arts

#It works if you take the map out but I want to keep it in
p <- ggplot()
p <- p + geom_point(data=mydata, hjust=0.5, vjust=-0.5, aes(x=long, y=lat,
         label=label), colour="gold2", size=4 )
p  + facet_grid(liberal_arts~.)
##################################################

R 2.14.1 (2011-12-22); windows OS

http://pastebin.com/iKi2xsgL

Cheers
Tyler

Hi Tyler:

Are you trying to construct a choropleth map? If so, then you should
probably install the development version of ggplot2-0.9.0 and consider
using geom_map() in the new version (it doesn't exist in 0.8.9). If
that's what you're after, let us know and we can show you how to
install it and get moving with it. The geom_map() help page and my
0.9.0 transition guide (which isn't quite ready for release to this
group yet but will probably be by next week) have an example using a
US map with a choropleth plot.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: faceting a map
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler:

The problem is that when you call facet_wrap(), there's no referent
data frame for liberal_arts. One way to resolve the problem is shown
below. I played around with a few other things, too, including aspect
ratios. Take the opts() code out and see what happens :)

library('ggplot2')
library('maps')
library('maptools')   # you forgot these...

mydata <- read.csv(file=url("http://dl.dropbox.com/u/6517578/tmp.csv"),
                   header=TRUE, row.names=1, sep=",")
all_states <- map_data("state")

# Don't know why you included the Dakotas since there are no points
# in either state - you could remove them WLOG and enlarge the faceted
# maps a bit

states <- subset(all_states, region %in% c( "illinois", "indiana", "iowa",
         "kentucky", "michigan", "minnesota","missouri", "north dakota",
         "ohio", "south dakota", "wisconsin" ))

# Use mydata as the data argument so that liberal_arts
# has a referent data frame when invoked
ggplot(mydata) +

       geom_polygon( data=states, aes(x=long, y=lat, group = group),

                     fill = 'grey 40', colour="skyblue" ) +
       geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat, label=label),
                    hjust=0.5, vjust=-0.5, colour="gold2", size=3 ) +
       opts(aspect.ratio = 1) +
       facet_wrap(~ liberal_arts, ncol = 1)

In 0.9.0, the extended spacing between the vertical axes and the axis
label is fixed. (See the attachments.)

The original blog post was fine because the poster didn't try to facet
by a variable - in that case, the ggplot() call with no arguments was
fine since each subsequent layer defined the data frame to be used  in
that layer. When you decided to experiment with faceting, you
neglected to realize that liberal_arts had no reference for ggplot()
to use, hence the error. Once you put mydata in the ggplot() call as
above, facet_wrap() can point back to it and retrieve the liberal_arts
variable.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Suggestion: simplification of scales by using higher level functions
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion: simplification of scales by using higher level functions
messages.body_plain:
(Moving to ggplot2-dev)

> What I meant by "do not produce what is expected" is that, in the
> stable version, the two examples above produce a plot with points at
> the same location but with no x axis.
> In the devel version there is an x axis but which is strangely formed:
>
>    d <- data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10))
>    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y))
>    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_x_discrete(breaks=c(0,0.5,1))
>    # produces a axis with breaks at 0 and 1 only and leaves a lot of
> blank space on the right of 1
>    ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + scale_x_date()
>    # produces an axis whose breaks depend on the current time (apparently)

Could you please file a bug for this?

> My impression is that ggplot would have enough information by looking
> at the class of the data associated with the scale. Now that may be a
> technical impossibility (cf above, the fact that the data is sometimes
> known only at render time).

Yes, it's the render time that's the problem.

>> If you don't know whether your
>> data is continuous or discrete you have bigger problems?
>
> I'm not saying it is hard for the user to know wether its data is
> discrete or continuous (or a date, or ...). I'm saying that it seems
> like it wouldn't be hard for ggplot to figure it out and spare the
> user having to think about it and write it explicitly. The whole
> concept of scales is difficult to apprehend for newcomers so anything
> that makes it more fluid, more intuitive seems very valuable to me.
> having to write _continuous or _discrete at the end of the scale name
> costs more than the few keystrokes it requires.

Again, my perspective is being explicit is slightly more painful in
the short-term, but is much easier in the long-term.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: plot point range on y axis
messages.subject_clean: plot point range on y axis
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You should provide a reproducible example so that respondents don't
have to generate their own to help you. That said, does the following
work?

library('ggplot2')   # will load plyr in 0.8.9, but not 0.9.0
# library('plyr')     # uncomment for 0.9.0

# fake data
DF <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:10], each = 20), y = rnorm(200))

# function to produce a CI and return it as a data frame, along with the mean
cifun <- function(d, level = 0.95) {
     quant <- (1 + level)/2
     n <- length(d$y)
     m <- mean(d$y, na.rm = TRUE)
     se <- sd(d$y, na.rm = TRUE)/sqrt(length(d$y))
     data.frame(mean = m, lcl = m - qt(quant, n - 1),
                 ucl = m + qt(quant, n - 1))
  }

v <- ddply(DF, .(gp), cifun)

# need to produce a data frame of intercepts if you have more than one
xints <- data.frame(x = c(-2, 2))

ggplot(v, aes(y = gp)) +
   geom_point(aes(x = mean), size = 3, colour = 'red') +
   geom_errorbarh(aes(x = mean, xmin = lcl, xmax = ucl),
                   colour = 'red', size = 1, width = 0.2) +
   geom_vline(data = xints, aes(xintercept = x), colour = 'blue', size = 1)

Notes:
(1) If you want a confidence level different from 0.95, you pass the
level = argument after the name of the function; e.g., ddply(DF,
.(gp), cifun, level = 0.8)
(2) If you only need one threshold, then you can set the intercept in
geom_vline(), e.g.,
    geom_vline(xintercept = 2.2, colour = 'blue', size = 1)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: plot nothing but only vline?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way, setting ylim().

mydf<-data.frame(pos=sample(100,size=12),grp=rep(1:3,each=4))
ggplot(mydf) + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = pos)) + facet_wrap(~ grp) +
ylim(0, 1)

In 0.8.9 this yields a 2 x 2 arrangement of facets; in 0.9.0, it
yields a 1 x 3 arrangement.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Writing an -log10 transformation
messages.body_plain:
On Feb 10, 1:23 pm, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> install.packages("devtools")
> library(devtools)
> dev_mode()
> install_github("ggplot2")
>
> library(ggplot2)
> library(scales)
> ?trans

Thank you for this.  The following worked a treat:
neglog_trans <- function (base = exp(1))
{
 trans <- function(x) -log(x, base)
 inv <- function(x) base^(-x)
 trans_new(str_c("neglog-", format(base)), trans, inv, log_breaks(base
= base), domain = c(1e-100, Inf))
}
neglog10_trans <- function () { neglog_trans(10) }

Regards, Freddie.

messages.subject: Unwanted extra legend
messages.body_plain:
Please run the following code for the first figure, and then compare
it with the second, which has an extra superfluous legend. Please tell
me (1) how to fix this, and (2) where I would find the documentation
that would have clarified this issue?

library( ggplot2 )
library( effects )
effectdf <- function( ... ){
	suppressWarnings( as.data.frame( effect( ... )))
}
data( ToothGrowth )
tg <- ToothGrowth
tg$dose.f <- factor( tg$dose )
m1 <- lm( len ~ supp * dose.f, data = tg )
m1.ef <- effectdf( 'supp:dose.f', m1 )
m1.ef$dose <- m1.ef$dose.f
m1.ef$dose.f <- factor(m1.ef$dose.f)
#############
#1st figure: dose is factor
#############
pd <- position_dodge( 0.1 )
p <- ggplot( m1.ef, aes( x = dose.f, y = fit,
   colour = supp ) )
p <- p + geom_point( position = pd )
p <- p + geom_line( aes( group = supp ), position = pd )
p <- p + xlab( 'dose' ) + ylab( 'mean(length)' )
p <- p + geom_errorbar(
   aes( ymin = lower, ymax = upper, width = 0.1 ),
   position = pd )
( p <- p + opts( legend.position = c( 0.66, 0.33 ) ) +
   scale_colour_discrete( name = 'supplement',
      breaks = c( 'OJ', 'VC' ),
      label = c( 'orange juice', 'ascorbic acid' ) ) )
#############
# 2nd figure: dose is continuous (but using points from 1st analysis)
#############
m2 <- lm( len ~ supp * dose, data = tg )
m2.ef <- effectdf( 'supp:dose', m2 )
pd <- position_dodge(0.05)
p <- ggplot( m2.ef, aes( x = dose, y = fit, colour = supp ) )
p <- p + xlab( 'dose' ) + ylab( 'mean(length)' )
p <- p + geom_point( data = m1.ef, aes( y = fit ),
   position = pd )
p <- p + geom_smooth(
   aes( y = fit, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = supp ),
   stat = 'identity', alpha = 0.2)
( p <- p + opts( legend.position = c( 0.66, 0.33 ) ) +
   scale_colour_discrete( name = 'supplement',
      breaks = c( 'OJ', 'VC' ),
      label = c( 'orange juice', 'ascorbic acid' ) ) )

messages.subject: Re: Unwanted extra legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

geom_smooth() was the source only because you mapped the fill
aesthetic to supp inside its aes(). By default, every mapped,
non-positional aesthetic (e.g, fill, color, size) generates its own
legend. A variable is mapped to an aesthetic inside an aes() call;
aesthetics can be set to constant values outside of aes(); e.g., size
= 3.

To merge two legends, they need to have the same legend title and the
same breaks, values and labels; that's usually done with
scale_aesthetic_manual(), as Ista pointed out (where 'aesthetic' is a
placeholder for the actual aesthetic).

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I don't know what's causing your problem, but you can use predict() to make predictions from the model, and then plot them with geom_line.

# Make the model
lqsmod <- lqs(bodywt~brainwt, data = msleep)
# Generate a sequence of x (brainwt) values and put them into a data frame
xval <- seq(min(msleep$brainwt, na.rm=TRUE), max(msleep$brainwt, na.rm=TRUE),
            length.out=100)
preddata <- data.frame(brainwt = xval)
# Predict bodywt values
preddata$bodywt <- predict(lqsmod, newdata = preddata)
# print
preddata

pq1 + geom_line(data=preddata)

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Loop
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It would help to have a small reproducible example, but some ways you
could avoid the problem might be:

(1) Don't use explicit for loops.
(2a) Convert the shapefile into a data frame using the fortify.sp()
function in ggplot2.
(2b) Melt the data, using the attribute variables as measure variables
(see ?reshape2::melt for details). Once the data are melted, the
variable names become factor levels, so you could then run d_ply() on
it. It's also useful to write a simple function that processes a
generic variable and then use that as the function to process with
d_ply().

Something along these lines might work:

library('reshape2')
library('plyr')
library('ggplot2')

# Inputs a generic data frame dat, outputs a pdf file
plotfun <- function(dat) {
   map <- qplot(PolyCoordsY, PolyCoordsX, data=dat,
                      group=Poly_Name , fill=variable, geom="polygon",

                      asp = 1, xlab="",ylab="")

   ggsave(map, file=paste(dat$variable, ".pdf"))
   invisible()
  }

# You will probably have to fortify the data first to make it a data frame.
# See fortify.sp() in ggplot2 for details, especially to identify the
# region polygons. Once you've made the conversion, let's say
# the name of the resulting data frame is setores_dom01.

# Melt the data:
setores.melt <- melt(setores_dom01, measure.vars = 15:255)

# Plot:
d_ply(setores_dom01, .(variable), plotfun)

The fortify step is the one you'll need to work out since we have no
information about the data structure of the shapefile. No guarantees
this will work as it's obviously untested.

Dennis

messages.subject: Plotting maps in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Greeting ggplot2 community,

I'm working to learn to plot maps in ggplot (well R for that matter but ggplot seems like the easiest connect point).  I recently came across a terrific map of downtown Houston Crime Data found here:

https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Crime-in-Downtown-Houston,-Texas-:-Combining-ggplot2-and-Google-Maps

I really liked the clarity and read David Kahle's instructions pretty carefully.  He warned at the end about:

"In making these kinds of plots, one might tempted to use the map raster file itself as a background. This method can be used to make map plots much more quickly than the methods described above. However, the method has one very significant disadvantage which, if not handled properly, can destroy the entire purpose of using the map. Specifically, by forcing the map image to be the background of the plot, the user bypasses the spatial referencing system dictated by the x and y-axes scales which are used to ensure consistency in spatial referencing."

Being ignorant I asked about these differences David was talking about at stack overflow and got a great response:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9255680/raster-map-vs-alternative

That got me searching through slides from Hadley Wickham's latest Webinar (Behind the Scenes)
http://www.revolutionanalytics.com/news-events/free-webinars/2012/ggplot2-with-hadley-wickham/?mkt_tok=3RkMMJWWfF9wsRoku6zJZKXonjHpfsXw6OUlWqWg38431UFwdcjKPmjr1YIBTcB0dvycMRAVFZl5nR5dDO%2BZaZRJ9fteBEyiTS%2F2jqY%3D

I was able to run Hadley's slide #24 that shows mapping using annotate_raster as suggested to me at stack overflow using this code:

########################################

library(reshape2)
library(RgoogleMaps)
library(ggmap)
theft <- subset(crime, offense == "theft" & lat > 29 & lat < 30.2 &
lon > -95.8)
lonr <- range(theft$lon)
latr <- range(theft$lat)
h_map <- GetMap.bbox(lonr, latr, size = c(1024, 1024))
h_raster <- as.raster(h_map$myTile)
benchplot(ggplot(theft, aes(lon, lat)) +
annotation_raster(h_raster, lonr[1], lonr[2], latr[1], latr[2]) +
geom_density2d(colour = "black"))
h_data <- melt(as.matrix(h_raster))
h_data$lat <- seq(latr[2], latr[1], length = 640)[h_data$Var1]
h_data$lon <- seq(lonr[1], lonr[2], length = 640)[h_data$Var2]
benchplot(ggplot(theft, aes(lon, lat)) +
geom_tile(aes(fill = value), data = h_data) +
scale_fill_identity() +
geom_density2d(colour = "black"))
########################################

In the GetMap.bbox line the size is set to 1024 x 1024.  When  I do so I get an error saying that the argument must be <= 640.  If I state 640 x 640 I'm fine.  The output though appears to be less clear(resolution) than the map of the crime data posted by David.  Is the map less clear (resolution) because I used 640 x 640?
Is the annotate_raster(as suggested to me on stack overflow) method able to produce a map of the same quality(resolution) that David presents in his Houston Crime data?  If so how?  If not what method(s) should I employ to generate a high resolution map?
The map generated from the webinar slide has all sorts of different axes.  I'm not sure what should stay and what should go there sot he map looks presentable.

messages.subject: [Q] Incorrect bin in geom_histogram
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am experiencing a odd problem. When I created a histogram using geom_histogram, I got a bin with negative values. The problem was that the variable I was creating a histogram for is a "fraction". Therefore, it was not possible to have a negative value, but somehow ggplot2 creates a bin with negative values.

When I created a histogram using a standard hist() function, I did not get any negative bin, of course. Also, the min. value returned from summary() was 0 as it should be.

Can anyone help me to resolve this issue?

Thanks in advance.

Young-Jin Lee

Hi Tyler -

Use the development version of ggmap off github; it already includes the geom_raster version (relying on what is now the dev version of ggplot2; that is, v.0.9.0).  Baptiste's answer on Stack Overflow was right on; now that they are there, they are certainly the way to go.  So to do that, you can simply do (foregoing the code Hadley used in the presentation).  The following will get you started :

library(devtools)
dev_mode()
install_github('scales')
install_github('ggplot2')
install_github('ggmap', username = 'dkahle')
library(ggmap)
qmap('the white house', fullpage = TRUE)
?ggmapplot

Let me know how it goes.

Cheers
david.

Hi!

A reproducible example and the results of running sessionInfo() are always needed to address these questions.

If you can't reproduce it, then at least provide the graph, the code, and some tabular description of the data that uses the same binning.

Without this no one can help you.

I will, however, take a stab in the dark and suggest you run update.packages() and make sure your R version is current (2.14.1) before trying to find more complex answers to your observation.

Rob

messages.subject: Transition guide from 0.8.9 to 0.9.0
messages.body_plain:
Greetings:

As many of you know, there is a new version of ggplot2 that has been
threatening to come out for the past few months. The anticipated
release date is March 1 if everything goes well with CRAN. Over the
past few weeks, I've been putting together a document, overseen by
development group members, that I hope will ease the transition from
ggplot2-0.8.9 to ggplot2-0.9.0. It covers the following topics:
    * basic changes in the package
    * new geoms
    * the new guides functionality that will give users more control
over the appearance of legend guides
    * a couple of new features in facet_grid()
    * examples using the new annotation functions
    * some coverage of the recent scales package and how it can be
used with ggplot2
    * lots of examples and pretty pictures :)

The document is attached to this mail, but discussions are ongoing as
to where it will have a more permanent home. I will let you know when
the location is determined, so that future updates can be cited rather
than attached as mail entries.

To run the code in this document, you'll need the development versions
of ggplot2 and scales. You will also need to have the following
packages installed from CRAN: plyr, reshape2, rgdal, maps, maptools,
rgeos, MASS, gridExtra and ReadImages. If you're not already using the
development version ggplot2-0.9.0 and you want to try out the code in
the document (also attached), here's how to get it:

(1) Install the devtools package from CRAN.
(2) [Optional...I think] Install Rtools from CRAN, in the same place
you grab the distribution binaries for your platform. (See the rtools
subdirectory.) Since neither ggplot2 nor scales uses any external C or
C++ code, this step may not be necessary.
(3) In a fresh R session:

library('devtools')
dev_mode()     # should reply dev_mode: ON - if not, do it again.
## only works if dev_mode is ON:

install_github("ggplot2")
install_github("scales")

# If both packages install without errors, then
library('ggplot2')    # note that plyr, reshape, etc. are NOT loaded!
library('scales')

...and start copying and pasting the code from the attached R file
into the session to replicate the plots. (Don't forget to load the
required packages first - they are not loaded inside the script.) If
the installation goes ka-bong, then try installing Rtools and repeat
step 3 above. On Windows, it's probably safer if you start the R
session by running it as Administrator.

The document was typeset using the recently released knitr package by
Yihui Xie. If you like the way it looks, visit the package website at
yihui.name/knitr <http://yihui.name/knitr>. I highly recommend it. (And thanks to Josh Wiley for
turning me onto it in December.)

Feedback and suggestions welcomed; if questions or problems arise,
don't be shy about asking. The objective is to have a working document
ready to go a few days before the release date.

I hope you find this guide useful as you move from ggplot2-0.8.9 to 0.9.0.

On behalf of the ggplot2 developers,
Dennis

messages.subject: Annotating geoms at creation time for better integration with gridSVG
messages.subject_clean: Annotating geoms at creation time for better integration with gridSVG
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have found ggplot2 + gridSVG + javascript to be a powerful
combination when producing interactive web-based charts.

After producing a plot with ggplot, I use the grid.garnish function
from gridSVG to annotate the exported svg xml with meta data that
helps with the interactivity in javascript (e.g. names and ids of the
points or rects in the plot so I can filter chart elements or display
names upon mouseover etc).

However, grid.garnish still requires some trial and error to annotate
the correct grobs, which isn't ideal when the grob creation order is
not necessarily the same as the source data for the plot (e.g. ggplot
sorts labels alphabetically).

To eliminate some of the guesswork, my colleague hit upon the idea of
modifying the geoms to take additional meta-data at the time of
creation (see the example below). This works well for 0.89, but
doesn't for the master 0.9 branch from github (it triggers  Error in
proto(GeomPoint, { : object 'GeomPoint' not found). If I import
GeomPoint then it complains about Toplevel not being found...

I have two questions:
1 - what changes do I need to make for this approach work for the
current 0.9 build (which I need for the new and excellent
annotate_raster functionality)
2 - is it possible to request an official method of annotating grobs
at the time of creation (the approach used by us of decorating the
gp() args is a total hack) . I imagine an optional garnish=T argument
that takes everything from within the aes() call and attaches it to a
list of meta data -  whatever additional meta data you want would be
added in the aes call and retained for later use.

Thanks in advance for your help.
Selwyn

##0.89 annotation example below
library(ggplot2)
library(gridSVG)

## extend the gp parameter in geom_point to take meta information that
can be extracted with grid.garnish (see example below)
## This works for 0.89, but triggers the following error in the
current 0.9 master from github:
## Error in proto(GeomPoint, { : object 'GeomPoint' not found

geom_point2 <- function (...) GeomPoint2$new(...)
GeomPoint2 <- proto(GeomPoint, {
  objname <- "point2"
  draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
{
    data <- remove_missing(data, na.rm,
                           c("x", "y", "size", "shape"), name =
"geom_point")
    if (empty(data)) return(zeroGrob())

    with(coordinates$transform(data, scales),
         ggname(.$my_name(), pointsGrob(x, y, size=unit(size, "mm"),
pch=shape,
                                        gp=gpar(col=alpha(colour,
alpha), fill = fill, fontsize = size * .pt,meta=meta)))
         )
  }
}
                    )

##example of usage that works in ggplot2 0.89
df = data.frame(id = 1:10,xval = runif(10),yval = runif(10))
ggplot(df,aes(xval,yval,meta=id)) + geom_point2()

grid.ls <http://grid.ls>()
grob_name = grid.get('geom_point2',grep=T)$name
grid.garnish(grob_name,meta = grid.get(grob_name)$gp$meta,group=F)
gridToSVG('test.svg') #inspecting the svg file you can see the ids
correctly assigned to each circle primitive

messages.subject: faceting heatmaps
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have a series of matrices, each one associated with two factors,
that I would like to plot as heatmaps in a pairwise grid fashion. I am
able to generate the heatmap for each individual grid and considered
laying them out via the grid.* functions.

But it seems more elegant to obtain a grid layout via faceting. While
the facets are pretty close to what I want, the problem is that
geom_tile generates heatmap based on the entire data.frame, rather
than individually for each facet. Instead what I would like to is to
have each heatmap be colored independently.

Some code:

library(ggplot2)

g1 <- matrix(runif(36), nrow=6)
g2 <- matrix(rnorm(36), nrow=6)
g3 <- matrix(rweibull(36, shape=0.5), nrow=6)
g <- rbind(
           data.frame( sid1='A', sid2='B', cbind( expand.grid(1:6,
1:6), resps=as.numeric(g1) )),
           data.frame( sid1='A', sid2='C', cbind( expand.grid(1:6,
1:6), resps=as.numeric(g2) )),
           data.frame( sid1='B', sid2='C', cbind( expand.grid(1:6,
1:6), resps=as.numeric(g3) )),
      )

names(g) <- c('sid1', 'sid2', 'r', 'c', 'resp')
base.size <- 9
p <- ggplot(g, aes(r,c))
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(fill = resp), colour='white')
p <- p + scale_fill_gradientn(colours=c('red', 'black'))
p <- p + theme_bw(base_size = base.size) + scale_x_continuous(expand =
c(0,0)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))
p + facet_grid(sid1~ sid2)

As you can see, the color scale for each heatmap is based on the
entire data range. How can I get this figure, but with each heatmap
colored independently?

facets in parallel.  I love that in plyr I can set a simple boolean in

On 13 Feb., 23:54, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Greetings:
>
> As many of you know, there is a new version of ggplot2 that has been
> threatening to come out for the past few months. The anticipated
> release date is March 1 if everything goes well with CRAN. Over the
> past few weeks, I've been putting together a document, overseen by
> development group members, that I hope will ease the transition from
> ggplot2-0.8.9 to ggplot2-0.9.0. It covers the following topics:
>     * basic changes in the package
>     * new geoms
>     * the new guides functionality that will give users more control
> over the appearance of legend guides
>     * a couple of new features in facet_grid()
>     * examples using the new annotation functions
>     * some coverage of the recent scales package and how it can be
> used with ggplot2
>     * lots of examples and pretty pictures :)
>
> The document is attached to this mail, but discussions are ongoing as
> to where it will have a more permanent home. I will let you know when
> the location is determined, so that future updates can be cited rather
> than attached as mail entries.
>
> To run the code in this document, you'll need the development versions
> of ggplot2 and scales. You will also need to have the following
> packages installed from CRAN: plyr, reshape2, rgdal, maps, maptools,
> rgeos, MASS, gridExtra and ReadImages. If you're not already using the
> development version ggplot2-0.9.0 and you want to try out the code in
> the document (also attached), here's how to get it:
>
> (1) Install the devtools package from CRAN.
> (2) [Optional...I think] Install Rtools from CRAN, in the same place
> you grab the distribution binaries for your platform. (See the rtools
> subdirectory.) Since neither ggplot2 nor scales uses any external C or
> C++ code, this step may not be necessary.
> (3) In a fresh R session:
>
> library('devtools')
> dev_mode()     # should reply dev_mode: ON - if not, do it again.
> ## only works if dev_mode is ON:
>
> install_github("ggplot2")
> install_github("scales")
>
> # If both packages install without errors, then
> library('ggplot2')    # note that plyr, reshape, etc. are NOT loaded!
> library('scales')
>
> ...and start copying and pasting the code from the attached R file
> into the session to replicate the plots. (Don't forget to load the
> required packages first - they are not loaded inside the script.) If
> the installation goes ka-bong, then try installing Rtools and repeat
> step 3 above. On Windows, it's probably safer if you start the R
> session by running it as Administrator.
>
> The document was typeset using the recently released knitr package by
> Yihui Xie. If you like the way it looks, visit the package website at
> yihui.name/knitr <http://yihui.name/knitr>. I highly recommend it. (And thanks to Josh Wiley for
> turning me onto it in December.)
>
> Feedback and suggestions welcomed; if questions or problems arise,
> don't be shy about asking. The objective is to have a working document
> ready to go a few days before the release date.
>
> I hope you find this guide useful as you move from ggplot2-0.8.9 to 0.9.0.
>
> On behalf of the ggplot2 developers,
> Dennis
>

Hello,

Similar to the question posted by Xiaoyu Yan yesterday, but I want to
align the width of x-axis of horizontal barplot among different
pages.
Would somebody tell me how to do?

Below I add an example of code what I want to draw. Real data is
several hundred of categories on y-axis, so I need to plot them on
different pages. Each label has different length. Padding by white
space doesn't work fine, as default font is not monospaced-font.

I noticed similar post was done before, and that Baptiste's advice,
using fixedSize.r, described seems just what I want. But I cannot
obtain fixedSize.r from http://ggextra.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/R/fiexedSize.r
(Forbidden even after I entered google.code password).
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/9db86987f6ab43b1/49f5dd643349dd87?lnk=gst&q=fixed+size+of+plot+area#49f5dd643349dd87

Thanks in advance,
Mickey

### barplot with different length of y-axis text for different pages
###

pdf_flag<-1	#to write to files 'test1.pdf' and 'test2.pdf'

y<-c(rep("long long long long label",2), rep("s",2))
val1<-c(5,10,2,9)
val2<-c(0.8,1,0.2,0.3)
categories<-c("cat1","cat2")
cat<-rep(categories,2)

dat<-data.frame(y,val1,val2,cat)

width<-1
row_n<-length(dat[,1])
category_n<-length(categories)
k_max<-floor((row_n-1)/width/category_n)+1
for (k in c(1:k_max)){
	i<-(k-1)*width*category_n +1
	j<-i+width*category_n -1
	dat_part<-dat[c(i:j),]
	dat_part[,'y']<-dat_part[,'y'][,drop=TRUE]
	if (pdf_flag){
		pdf_f<-paste('test',k,'.pdf',sep='')
			#test1.pdf, test2.pdf
		pdf(file=pdf_f)
	}
	q1<-qplot(y,val1,data= dat_part,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")
+coord_flip()
	q2<-qplot(y,val2,data= dat_part,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")
+coord_flip()
+opts(axis.title.y=theme_blank(),axis.text.y=theme_blank())

	grid.arrange(q1 + opts(legend.position="none"),q2,ncol=2)

	if(pdf_flag){
		dev.off()
	}
}

Christophe

>    for(i in dataNames) {
>      thisData<-coffs[[i]]
>      last_plot() + geom_line(aes(y = thisData, colour = i))
>    }
>    last_plot() + ylab("Total Chargeoffs")
> }
>
> coffs is a data.frame.
>
> I get the following error:
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'thisData' not found
>
> As little as I know about environments in R I am pretty sure that the
> geom_line in the loop is not able to see the thisData variable.
>
> Any help you could provide would be appreciated. I would be surprised if
> there wasn't a way to pass the data into the geom_line function without
> using environments. Of course I have been wrong once or twice in the past.
> :)
>
> Note that geom_line also can't see the input variable "coffs".

You are confusing what should be passed to the aesthetic in geom_line.
It should be a reference to a column of data in the data.frame, either
as an unevaluated variable or a character string. You are trying to pass
a vector of data.

graphChargeOffs2<-function(coffs) {
   ggplot(coffs, aes(levels))
   dataNames<-names(coffs)[!names(coffs) == "levels"]
   for(i in dataNames) {

     last_plot() + geom_line(aes_string(y = i))

   }
   last_plot() + ylab("Total Chargeoffs")
}

Note I am using aes_string rather than aes because the name of the
column which contains the data is held in the string `i`. Also, this
does not color the lines differently, which I think was something you
wanted.

The reason there is so much problems getting this to work is that this
isn't the natural way to approach the problem in ggplot2. For something
like this, you are better off working with melted (long) data. With
that, you don't need a loop at all.

library("reshape2")

graphChargeOffs3<-function(coffs) {
   coffs.m <- melt(coffs, id.vars="levels")
   ggplot(coffs.m, aes(x=levels, y=value, colour=variable)) +
     geom_line() +
     ylab("Total Chargeoffs")
}

messages.subject: Re: Graph over graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's a simple example using ggplot2-0.9.0, which you need for the
annotation_custom() function:

library('ggplot2')   # ggplot2-0.9.0
DF <- data.frame(x = rnorm(200))
# save the histogram as a ggplot object
p1 <- ggplot(DF, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)
# turn it into a graphical object (grob)
p2 <- ggplotGrob(p1)
# annotation_custom() lets you add a grob to a ggplot
ggplot(DF, aes(x = 0.2, y = x)) + theme_bw() +
    geom_boxplot(fill = 'blue', alpha = 0.2) +
    xlim(0, 1) +
    annotation_custom(p2, xmin = 0.5, xmax = 1, ymin = 0, ymax = 2)

If you don't have ggplot2-0.9.0, here's how to add it to your R
packages without breaking the current CRAN version (0.8.9):

library('devtools')   # install first if necessary
dev_mode()     # should reply dev_mode ON
install_github('ggplot2')  # wait for it to install
library('ggplot2')

Installing packages while dev_mode() is on allows you to maintain a
CRAN version of a package and a development version simultaneously.
The help pages are housed in separate directories on your machine.
When dev_mode is ON and you load a package, it will load the
development version if it exists; when dev_mode is OFF, it will load
the CRAN version if you have both CRAN and development versions
installed. In the above code chunk, ggplot2 is installed while
dev_mode is ON, so it's getting the development version from GitHub;
subsequent loading of the package means that the development version
is in use. (Note: if you install the development version of a package
while dev_mode is OFF, it will overwrite the CRAN version in
$R_HOME/library, so be careful.)

You can tell which version is loaded by calling packageVersion(): for
the development version,
packageVersion('ggplot2')
[1] ‘0.9.0’

For more on this topic, see the transition guide from 0.8.9 to 0.9.0
that I posted to this group on Monday, IIRC. If you don't have it,
check out
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/msg/2a6ab7a72e658c6d

In the document, look for section 4 on new annotation functions.

It's also possible to do this kind of thing in 0.8.9 but it requires
playing with grid viewports; see section 8.4.1 of Hadley's ggplot2
book. If you don't have access to it, you can find the code for that
section at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/book/polishing.r . The code of
interest is toward the bottom of the file starting with a comment that
begins 'Three simple graphics...'

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

(a) don't attach data frames if you don't have to;
(b) qplot() has a data argument, whose purpose is to temporarily
attach the data frame until qplot() completes; this is documented on
the help page and illustrated in the free on-line chapter regarding
qplot(), found at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/book/qplot.pdf
It's safer to use the data = argument of qplot() than to attach a data
frame to a session.

Try

library('ggplot2')
qplot(hp, wt, data = mtcars)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = 1, fill = factor(cyl))) +
    geom_bar(position = 'stack', binwidth = 0.2)

These work for me on a Win 7, 64-bit system. I tried parts of your
code on my system and they also worked. To make a sensible stacked
(percentage) bar plot, it's useful to have two factors in the plot
call: one to provide individual bars for the factor of interest, the
other to perform the stacking. The stacking variable is typically
associated with an aesthetic and will produce a legend by default.
This is a rather inane example, but it illustrates the point; you can
think of it as a way of checking that the design giving rise to the
data is balanced:

ggplot(OrchardSprays, aes(x = treatment, fill = factor(colpos))) +
     geom_bar(position = 'stack')

As far as the error message is concerned, I'm wondering if you have
one or more objects in your workspace that conflict with the attached
mtcars data frame (one reason why attaching data frames is often not a
good idea). I'd look for potential conflicts between the objects in
your workspace, the variables in the attached data frame and possibly
with the functions in the ggplot2 package. A good rule of thumb is not
to save objects in your workspace but rather to create and save script
files that can quickly reproduce the objects  when necessary. In other
words, don't clutter up the workspace with objects other than the ones
you're working on at the moment.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Plotting asterix for significance in facetted bar plot
messages.body_plain:
You can use geom_text, and map a text column to 'label':

dat <- data.frame(name=c("a","b","a","c","a","b","d","c"),
                  val=c(1,-1.2,2.2,0.9,-0.7,2.4,-2.3,0.6),
                  sd=c(0.2,0.3,0.25,0.2,0.25,0.6,0.56,0.2),
                  p=c(0.09,0.1,0.02,0.1,0.2,0.001,0.001,0.6),
                  grp=c("A","A","B","B","C","C","C","C"))

dat$star <- ""
dat$star[dat$p <= .05]  <- "*"
dat$star[dat$p <= .01]  <- "**"
dat$star[dat$p <= .001] <- "***"

ggplot(dat, aes(x=name,y=val,width=0.5,ymin=val-sd,ymax=val+sd)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +

  geom_errorbar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +

  geom_text(aes(label=star), colour="red", vjust=0, size=10) +
  facet_grid(. ~ grp, scales="free_x", space="free",margin=FALSE)

A few notes:
- I set vjust=0, so that the baseline of the text is at the y value. You could instead do something like aes(y=val+.2) to shift the text up a little.
- This looks a little funny with the positive and negative bars, since the stars end up inside the negative bars. If your data is really like this, I'd suggest not using bars... but if you must, then you could create a new column for y positions of the text, and for negative values, adjust the y value so that the text is outside the bar.

Hope this helps!
-Winston

messages.subject: ternary plot in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hello -- does anyone know of a way to draw a ternary plot in ggplot2 ?
[ http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_plot ]

I tried a few of the packages listed by:
library(sos)
findFn('ternary plot')

[ see prev post @ http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/4402c825551a2c06
]

Some of them I can't get to work, others the output doesn't look as
good as a ggplot!

What I wish to do is essentially draw a 3-way scatterplot based on one
row of numbers such as the following:
x    y    z
0.1    0.3    0.6

Any help would be much appreciated. Andrew

messages.subject: Re: figure alignment among different pages
messages.body_plain:
I solved my problem as below, which mostly stands on align.plots
supplied by Tengfei Yin in the post 'ggplot2 figure alignment', thank
you.

Thank you Baptiste. The code helped me to glimpse the way how ggplot2
works.

Also thanks to the ggplot 0.9.0 development team and Dennis Murphy who
told us the info, as 0.9.0 positions x-labels properly center-
justified relative to the plot region, that is, without including the
region of title and text of y-axis.

Mickey

	# < Background >
	#  Functions described below stand on the function 'align.plots'
supplied by Tengfei Yin.
	#   As the functions below become complicated to me myself, I also
cited original align.plots at the end for convenience.
	#   Original align.plots can be found at:
	#    https://github.com/tengfei/ggbio/blob/master/R/tracks.R#L78
	#    Related post: http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/273658d59066a1a3

	# < Points of this code different from 'align.plots' >
	# 1. It aligns y-axis on different pages.
	# 2. It can plot multiple columns.

	# < How this code works >
	# 1. Check the maximum width among the all data.
	# 2. Pass the max value to plot.aligned.plots.per.page <http://plot.aligned.plots.per.page> to draw each
page.

	# < Memo about this code >
	# 1. When the maximum length of y-labels are extremely long.
	#  1-1. File size may need to manually set.
	#        e.g. In the example below, pdf(file=pdf_f,width=13,height=8)
works fine, whereas width=8,height=8 doesn't.
	#  1-2. Need manual tuning to find appropriate ratio of width of
panels of columns.
	#        To do so, assign appropriate numbers for
'widths=unit(c(2,1), "null")' argument
	#        of gl<-grid.layout() line of plot.aligned.plots.per.page <http://plot.aligned.plots.per.page>.
	# 2. The height of the last page need to be tuned so that interval
between samples should be the same as other pages.
	#     Below, I added dummy (empty) data named 'NA1','NA2',... (and
will remove them on drawing software).
	#     Another way (not coded nor tested) would be assign 'ratio' to
the heights parameter
	#      of plot.aligned.plots.per.page <http://plot.aligned.plots.per.page> for the last page,
	#      that is, modify heights = unit(rep(1, nrow)) to heights =
unit(rep(1*ratio, nrow)).
	#      This is appoximate way as this does not count the height of x-
label region and margins at top and bottom.

	# < Not done >
	# *Aligning right side does not work (hence comment-outed in the
example),
	#   as ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots[[1]])) of f_legends needs
layers first.

	# < Memo to use this code >
	# *Need ggplot2 0.9.0
	#  1. To install ggplot2 0.9.0 as development mod along with current
0.8.9,
	#      see Dennis Murphy's comments:
	#      http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/58e64ed9db2782f5
	#      http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/msg/2a6ab7a72e658c6d
	#   (1) Install the devtools package from CRAN.
	#        install.packages('devtools')
	#   (2) In a fresh R session:
	#        library('devtools')
	#        dev_mode()     # should reply dev_mode: ON - if not, do it
again.
	#        ## only works if dev_mode is ON:
	#        install_github("ggplot2")
	#        # If the package install without errors, then
	#        library('ggplot2')    # note that plyr, reshape, etc. are
NOT loaded!
	#   (3) Check version
	#        packageVersion('ggplot2')
	#        #[1] ‘0.9.0’
	#
	#  2. 0.8.9 doesn't work for the following two points,
	#   (1) ggplot_gtable used for checking widths.right is unavailable
under 0.8.9.
	#   (2) 0.9.0 center-justifies axis.title.x with the range of xlim
(or plot area, I'm not sure),
	#         whereas 0.8.9 center-justifies with the sum of
axis.title.y, axis.text.y and the range of xlim.

use_dev_mode_flag<-1
if (use_dev_mode_flag){
	library('devtools')
	dev_mode()
}

library("ggplot2")	#Need ggplot2 0.9.0.
packageVersion('ggplot2')
	#First check version
library("grid")	#For grid.layout

	### Internal functions to calculate width.left ###
	# (called twice from get.width.left.max and get.width.left.cols).
f_ytitles<-function(dots){
		lapply(dots, function(.g){
		grob.y.text<-getGrob(.g, "axis.title.y.text", grep = TRUE)
		if(!is.null(grob.y.text))
			editGrob(grob.y.text, vp = NULL)
		else
			ggplot2:::zeroGrob()
	})
}
f_ylabels<-function(dots){
	lapply(dots, function(.g){
		grob.y.text<-getGrob(.g, "axis.text.y.text", grep = TRUE)
		if(!is.null(grob.y.text))
			editGrob(grob.y.text, vp = NULL)
		else
			ggplot2:::zeroGrob()
	})
}
f_widths.left<-function(ytitles, ylabels){
	widths.left<-mapply(`+`, e1 = lapply(ytitles, grobWidth),
		e2 = lapply(ylabels, grobWidth), SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
}

	### Internal functions to calculate width.right ###
	# (called twice from get.width.right.max and get.width.right.cols).
f_legend.pos<-function(dots){
	lapply(dots,function(x) {
		if (is.null(x$options$legend.pos)) "right"
		else x$options$legend.pos
    })
}
f_legends<-function(dots){
	lapply(dots,function(.g){
		gt<-ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(.g))
		idx<-grep("guide-box", gt$layout$name)
		l.pos<-ggplot2:::plot_theme(.g)$legend.position
			## ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots0[[1]]))$layout
		if(length(idx)){
			if(l.pos == "right"){
				gt$widths[gt$layout[idx,"r"]]
			}else{
				warning("only support right legend now")
				grobWidth(ggplot2:::zeroGrob())
			}
			## editGrob(gt$grobs[[idx]], vp = NULL)
		}else{
			grobWidth(ggplot2:::zeroGrob())
		}
	})
}
f_strips<-function(dots){
	lapply(dots, function(.g) {
		cc<-.g$children
		vstrips<-cc[grepl("^strip-right",names(cc))]
		if (length(vstrips)>0)
			editGrob(vstrips[[1]],vp=NULL)
		else ggplot2:::zeroGrob()
	})
}
f_widths.right<-function(legends,legend.pos,strips){
	widths.right<-mapply(function(g,lp,s) {
		g + grobWidth(s)
	}, legends,legend.pos,strips,  SIMPLIFY=FALSE)
}

	### Get max width_left of all data first ###
get.width.left.max<-function (..., vertical = TRUE,
                          heights = unit(rep(1, nrow), "null"))
{
		# Calculate for every columns, not for rows.
	if (!vertical) stop("only vertical alignment implemented")

	dots0<-list(...)
	nrow<-length(dots0)
	dots<-lapply(dots0, ggplotGrob)

	ytitles<-f_ytitles(dots)
	ylabels<-f_ylabels(dots)

	widths.left<-f_widths.left(ytitles, ylabels)

	widths.left.max<-max(do.call(unit.c, widths.left))
	widths.left.max
}

	### Get max width_right of all data first ###
get.width.right.max<-function (..., vertical = TRUE,
                          heights = unit(rep(1, nrow), "null"))
{
		# Calculate for every columns, not for rows.
	if (!vertical) stop("only vertical alignment implemented")

	dots0<-list(...)
	nrow<-length(dots0)
	dots<-lapply(dots0, ggplotGrob)

	legends.pos<-f_legend.pos(dots)
	legends<-f_legends(dots)
	strips<-f_strips(dots)

	widths.right<-f_widths.right(legends,legend.pos,strips)

	widths.right.max<-max(do.call(unit.c, widths.right))
	widths.right.max
}

	###
get.widths.left.cols<-function(dots.cols){
	ytitles.cols<-lapply(dots.cols,f_ytitles)
	ylabels.cols<-lapply(dots.cols,f_ylabels)

	widths.left.cols<-mapply(f_widths.left,ytitles.cols,ylabels.cols,
SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
	widths.left.cols
}
get.widths.right.cols<-function(dots.cols){
	legend.pos.cols<-lapply(dots.cols,f_legend.pos)
	legends.cols<-lapply(dots.cols,f_legends)
	strips.cols<-lapply(dots.cols,f_strips)

	widths.right.max<-mapply(f_widths.right,legends,legend.pos,strips,
SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
	widths.right.max
}

plot.aligned.plots.per.page <http://plot.aligned.plots.per.page><-function (
	qss,
	widths.left.max.cols,
	vertical = TRUE,
	heights = unit(rep(1, nrow), "null")
) {
	if (!vertical) stop("only vertical alignment implemented")

	ncol<- length(qss)	# Two in the example, i.e. left and right.

	dots00.cols<-lapply(qss,list)	# I don't know how to use '(...)' yet.
	#dots00<-list(...)
	nrow<-length(dots00.cols[[1]])	# One row in the example case.

	dots.cols<-lapply(dots00.cols,function(dots0)
{lapply(dots0,ggplotGrob)})

			# Initialize output device.
	#gl <- grid.layout(nrow = nrow, ncol = ncol, heights=heights,
widths=unit(c(2,1), "null"))
		# When the maximum of y-labels are exremely long, need to tune the
ratio of panel width among columns.
	gl<-grid.layout(nrow = nrow, ncol = ncol, heights=heights)
	vp<-viewport(layout = gl)
	pushViewport(vp)

	widths.left.cols<-get.widths.left.cols(dots.cols)
	# widths.right.cols<-get.widths.right.cols(dots.cols)
		#Aligning right side does not work,
		# as ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots[[1]])) of f_legends needs
layers first.

	for (ii in seq_along(dots.cols[[1]])) {
			# From left to right, then top to bottom,
			#  although only 1 row per page in the example.
		for (j in seq_along(dots.cols)){
			pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = ii, layout.pos.col = j))
			pushViewport(viewport(
				x = unit(0, "npc") + widths.left.max.cols[[j]] -
widths.left.cols[[j]][[ii]],
				width = unit(1, "npc")
					- widths.left.max.cols[[j]] + widths.left.cols[[j]][[ii]],
					# - widths.left.max.cols[[j]] + widths.left.cols[[j]][[ii]]
					# - widths.right.max + widths.right[[ii]],
		#Aligning right side does not work,
		# as ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots[[1]])) of f_legends needs
layers first.
				just = "left"))
			grid.draw(dots.cols[[j]][[ii]])
			upViewport(2)
		}
	}
}

pdf_flag<-1 #0     # To write to files 'test1.pdf' and 'test2.pdf'

	### Start of making test data.frame 'dat' and categories ###
row_types<-c("long long long long long5 long long long long long10
long long long long long15 long label","s","s2","s3")
y<-as.vector(apply(matrix(row_types,byrow=F,nrow=1), 2, function(str)
{rep(str,2)}))
#y<-c(rep("long long long long label",2), rep("s",2))
val1<-c(5,10,2,9,3,3,4,4.5)
val2<-c(0.8,1,0.2,0.3,0.1,0.15,0.6,0.65)
categories<-c("cat1","cat2")	# Use later
cat<-rep(categories,length(row_types))

dat<-data.frame(y,val1,val2,cat)	# Use later
	### End of making 'dat' ###

	### Start of calculating the max width.left and width.right of all
data. ###
	#
	#  Make object of all data first to this purpose.
	#  Do this caluculation for every columns.
	#   (Maybe only left-most one may be necessary when I don't plot
either axis.title.y or axis.text.y, but I'm not sure.)
q1all<-qplot(y,val1,data=dat,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")
+coord_flip()+ opts(legend.position="none")
	# For column 1 (left side plot)
q2all<-qplot(y,val2,data=dat,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")
+coord_flip()
+opts(axis.title.y=theme_blank(),axis.text.y=theme_blank())
	# For column 2 (right side plot)

qss0<-c(list(q1all),list(q2all))
widths.left.max.cols<-lapply(qss0, get.width.left.max)
# widths.right.max.cols<-lapply(qss0, get.width.right.max)
		#Aligning right side does not work,
		# as ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots[[1]])) of f_legends needs
layers first.
	### End of calculating the max width.left and width.right of all
data. ###

col_n<-2	# How many types of plot to draw left to right.
row_n<-length(dat[,1])	# How many data to plot in total.
width<-3	# How many rows of plot per page.
#width<-2
category_n<-length(categories)	# How many samples/categories in one
plot.
k_max<-floor((row_n-1)/width/category_n)+1	# How many pages in total.

for (k in c(1:k_max)){	# For each page..
	i<-(k-1)*width*category_n+1
	j<-k*width*category_n
	dat_part<-dat[c(i:j),]	# Data for each page

	dat_part[,'y']<-dat_part[,'y'][,drop=TRUE]

	if (k == k_max){	# When the last page..
		n_row_isna<-length(dat_part[is.na <http://is.na>(dat_part[,'y']),][,'y'])
		if (n_row_isna){
			dat_part[is.na <http://is.na>(dat_part[,'y']),]['cat']<-rep(categories,
n_row_isna / category_n)
				#Otherwise color may be different from others.

			levs_isna0<-paste('NA',seq(1, n_row_isna / category_n),sep='')
#labels 'NA1', 'NA2',...
			levels(dat_part[,'y'])<-c(levels(dat_part[,'y']),levs_isna0)
			levs_isna1<-as.vector(apply(matrix(levs_isna0,byrow=F,nrow=1), 2,
function(str){rep(str, category_n)}))
			dat_part[is.na <http://is.na>(dat_part[,'y']),]['y']<-levs_isna1

		}
	}

	q1<-qplot(y,val1,data= dat_part,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")

+coord_flip()+ opts(legend.position="none",axis.title.y=theme_blank())

	q2<-qplot(y,val2,data= dat_part,geom="bar",fill=cat,position="dodge")
+coord_flip()
+opts(axis.title.y=theme_blank(),axis.text.y=theme_blank())

	if (pdf_flag){
		pdf_f<-paste('test',k,'.pdf',sep='')
			#test1.pdf, test2.pdf

		#pdf(file=pdf_f)
		pdf(file=pdf_f,width=13,height=8)
		#pdf(file=pdf_f,width=8,height=8)
	}

	#grid.arrange(q1 + opts(legend.position="none"),q2,ncol=2)
		#see what it looks like by simply drawing a page by this function.

	qss<-c(list(q1),list(q2))
		# q1 for left panel, q2 for right panel
		# In the example, only one row in one page.
	plot.aligned.plots.per.page <http://plot.aligned.plots.per.page>(
		qss,
		widths.left.max.cols
		# widths.left.max.cols,
		# widths.right.max.cols
		#Aligning right side does not work,
		# as ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(dots[[1]])) of f_legends needs
layers first.
	)

	if(pdf_flag){
		dev.off()
	}
}

messages.subject: Vertical lines plotting outside x-bounds
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I've run into a conflict between using an external data.frame to add
additional data to a plot and the scales argument in facet_wrap(). The
example with the comment should illustrate this problem:

require(ggplot2)
## Generate the dataframe for plotting
df <- data.frame(a1=runif(20), Date=c(1990:2001, 1990:1997),
f=c("A","A","A","A","A","A","A","A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B","B","B"))
## Generate the dataframe for the lines annotating the plot
lines.df <- data.frame(Date=c(1992,1996,2000),Event=c("Cond1","Cond2","Cond3"))

## The plot itself.
ggplot(df, aes(x=Date, y=a1)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(data=lines.df, aes(xintercept=Date, linetype=Event)) +
  facet_wrap(~f, scales="free_x")

## Now my problem is that in facet "B", I've plotted a vertical line
at the year "2000" outside the x-bound of the original data set. Of
course this is exactly what I asked
## ggplot2 to do but I was wondering if anyone could think of a way to
limit the lines.df to only plot when it falls within the range of data
dictated by the "main"
## dataframe (df). Basically in this example, I don't want to plot the
year "2000" vertical line in the B facet but I do want to keep it in
the A facet and generally I
## the flexibility to plot "external" data onto a plot without
altering the original x (or y) limits.

Thanks so much in advance!

Sam

messages.subject: Re: Wrong position of x-axis text
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Strangely (under both 0.8.9 and 0.9.0), behavior of vjust changes
'global' and 'local' depending on angle=** parameter ('local' when
angle is 0 or 90; 'global' when angle is not 0 or 90 (i.e.
angle=60,angle=45 etc). On the other hand, hjust is always 'local'
irrespective of angle value.

Back to the question of erich, 'hjust=1,vjust=1' with 'angle=45' works
properly in my environment, if you want to make a plot similar as the
one you linked to, i.e. the rightmost of the labels are aligned below
ticks. Both under 0.8.9 and 0.9.0 worked; 0.9.0 is preferable in that
y-title is properly positioned.

> Even worse, the change in the horizontal position will depend on the
> length of the labels. So, it's very difficult to the get the positions right
> with unequal label lengths.

In my opinion, it's reasonable that if hjust=0.5, the 0.5 position of
the label, i.e. the center, is below the tick, and if 0.8, the 0.8
position of the label is below the tick.

The point is that it changes both horizontal and vertical in global
coordinate when angle!={0,90}, as hjust is applied to local. This is a
straightforward interpolation of two extremes, hjust=0 and hjust=1 (I
guess both results are reasonable for us).
But for 0<hjust<1 when angle!={0,90}, we may want to align labels as
center-justified horizontally in global coordinate but still put
labels 'proper' location below ticks (vertically justified at the top
in global coordinate). To do so, global hjust=0.5 and global vjust=1
are necessary, but it seems there're no way to indicate hjust/vjust to
be global or local.

I add examples that clarify those cases below.

Mickey

use_dev_mode_flag<-1
if (use_dev_mode_flag){
	library('devtools')
	dev_mode()
}

library("ggplot2")	#Need ggplot2 0.9.0.
packageVersion('ggplot2')
	#First check version

	### Start of making test data.frame 'dat' and categories ###
row_types<-c("very long long long long long5 long long long long
long10 long long long long long15 long label","s","s2","s3")
y<-as.vector(apply(matrix(row_types,byrow=F,nrow=1), 2, function(str)
{rep(str,2)}))
val1<-c(5,10,2,9,3,3,4,4.5)
categories<-c("cat1","cat2")
cat<-rep(categories,length(row_types))

dat<-data.frame(y,val1,val2,cat)
	### End of making 'dat' ###

	### Clear examples ###
# 1. vjust=1 moves whole labels upward, justified both horizontal and
vertical by local hjust=0.5.
	#We need global hjust=0.5 and global vjust=1 when we want to align
labels as center-justified horizontally but still put labels 'proper'
location below ticks.
	# Presently, vjust is global and hjust is local.
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=60,hjust=0.5, vjust=0.5))
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=60,hjust=0.5, vjust=1))

# 2. Behavior of vjust suddenly changes from angle=90 to 89
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90,hjust=1,vjust=0))
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=89,hjust=1,vjust=0))
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=60,hjust=1,vjust=0))

# 3. Positive value of vjust move labels rightward in global
coordinate under angle=90. I imagined this is negative direction in
local coodinate.
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90,hjust=1,vjust=0))
qplot(y,val1,data= dat,geom="bar",fill=cat)+
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=90,hjust=1,vjust=2))

messages.subject_clean: re-creating violin plot from learnR blog
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to create some violin plots and I keep getting an error

Error: Non-continuous variable supplied to scale_y_continuous.

I'm following the examples on learn R blog <http://learnr.wordpress.com/2009/07/02/ggplot2-version-of-figures-in-lattice-multivariate-data-visualization-with-r-part-3/>, and I notice that those examples that probably worked in the past, are no longer working. Any thoughts on how to go about this problem? This is the full code that produces the above error:

library(latticeExtra)
data(gvhd10)
p <- ggplot(gvhd10, aes(x = log(FSC.H), y = Days))
pg <- p + geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ..density.., ymin = -..density..),
    stat = "density") + facet_grid(Days ~ ., as.table = F,
    scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "log(Forward Scatter)",
    y = "Days Past Transplant")
pg

# same plot in lattice
pl <- bwplot(Days ~ log(FSC.H), gvhd10, panel = panel.violin,
     box.ratio = 3, xlab = "log(Forward Scatter)", ylab = "Days Past Transplant")
print(pl)

Cheers,
Roman

On 2/18/2012 8:07 AM, kw wrote:
> Brian,
>    Thanks a lot. I have been using R for a few years now and my foray into
> ggplot is the first time that I ever saw the "melt" function.
>
> I will use melt from now on for this type of graph and hopefully others.
>
> Just for completeness do you know of any way to get a different colour for
> each line in my original program?

The problem with getting a different colour is that one aesthetic (y)
was being specified by a string variable, the value of which is the name
of the column to be used and the other aesthetic (colour) was being
specified as a literal character. The first requires aes_string, the
second, aes. And there isn't a straightforward way to combine multiple
aes's.

However, thinking about it some more (and having spent some time looking
at how aes's are implemented), here is a very hackish way to get it to
work. It's hackish in that it relies on implementation details of aes
(which are not guaranteed by the interface) and the fact that you are
using a literal string for one of the aes.

graphChargeOffs2<-function(coffs) {
   ggplot(coffs, aes(levels))
   dataNames<-names(coffs)[!names(coffs) == "levels"]
   for(i in dataNames) {

     aess <- aes_string(y=i)
     aess["colour"] <- i
     last_plot() + geom_line(aess)

   }
   last_plot() + ylab("Total Chargeoffs")
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Short answer: no. Hadley did mention in the webinar (as did David
Smith in an earlier post on his Revolutions blog) that this is ongoing
research work in collaboration with a student and the Revolution R
people. I have no knowledge of the arrangement, but there may be
restrictions on what Hadley can impart about this project. Some people
have recently tried to download a nascent package on Hadley's GitHub
site but have found that it's not in a workable state yet. Similar
questions have been raised here in the week or so since the webinar
took place.

I have no idea what exactly he is doing to get that graphic, but my
first guess would be that the data are partitioned into 'packets'
according to a spatial configuration (e.g., a rectangular grid), the
statistical transformation is applied to the data values inside each
rectangle/polygon (e.g, a density plot) via one of the **ply()
functions, where in the function to be applied, a grid grob is created
in each iteration.  Then something like annotation_raster() or
annotation_custom() is applied sequentially to position the collection
of such grobs for final rendering at the appropriate size. If the
number of observations in a rectangle fall below a certain threshold,
no statistical transformation, and hence no grob, is created.
Basically, it looks like a generalization of geom_tile() where images
replace individual colors. It's not hard to extend the density plot
example to any 2D graphic, including a scatterplot; in that event, the
graphic becomes a generalization of a coplot. The aforementioned
annotation_* functions are available in the current development
version of ggplot2.

The algorithm for producing the structure of the graphic doesn't
appear to be that hard; the challenge is to do it in a 'reasonable'
amount of time. For example, a million points distributed over a 100 x
100 grid might take a while to process. With millions or billions of
data points and many rectangular/polygonal partitions of a 2D data
space, code efficiency is a high priority...and it's a lot easier to
talk about efficient code than it is to produce it. (Of course, as
Hadley has mentioned before, the simplest way to improve code
efficiency is to buy a bigger, faster computer :)

I don't pretend to speak for Hadley and have no involvement with the
research, so take my comments for what they're (not) worth. You could
probably find a way to code up a Q & D version of that plot with the
upcoming version of ggplot2 and some knowledge of grid graphics, but
expect that it might take a while to render if you have a large data
set.

Dennis
