messages.subject: Re: Spiral visualisation of time series data
messages.subject_clean: Spiral visualisation of time series data
messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Feb-17, at 18:10 , Tony Hirst wrote:
>
> I've just been tinkering with a few ways of visualising Twitter timeline data using ggplot ( http://blog.ouseful.info/2012/02/17/visualising-twitter-user-timeline-activity-in-r/ ) and as I was doing so, I was reminded of the use of interactive spirals as a technique for seeking periodicity, as in http://eagereyes.org/techniques/spirals
>
> Leaving aside interactive features (for the moment?!;-), is there a documented way of generating an N-sided spiral over eg day binned time series data using ggplot2?

There is no pre-made method but you can get close enough with geom_tile in polar coordinates. It is close visually, but not a spiral (it is just rows of values, to get a spiral, one should compute the coordinates of each tile so that they slightly increase in y direction). Here is a "reproduction" of http://eagereyes.org/techniques/spirals with the devel version of ggplot2 (polar coordinates behave differently in the release version):

# get the devel version of ggplot2
library("devtools")
install_github("ggplot2")
library("ggplot2")

# Idea from
# http://eagereyes.org/techniques/spirals
# Data from
# http://www.dartmouth.edu/~chance/teaching_aids/data/birthday.txt

d <- read.table("http://www.dartmouth.edu/~chance/teaching_aids/data/birthday.txt", col.names=c("date", "n"))
# create a time coordinate easier to work with
d$day <- seq(from=0, along.with=d$date)
# NB: the plot will only work with a regular time coordinate so if that's not the case, then you should bin the time series beforehand

# plot the series, just to check
qplot(day, n, data=d, geom="path")

# period to test
p <- 21

# remove period from time coordinate
d$x <- d$day %% p

# compute number of periods elapsed
d$y <- floor(d$day / p)

# "bar" version
pBar <- ggplot(d) +
    # plot tiles of the appropriate colour
    geom_tile(aes(x=x, y=y, fill=n)) +
    # use approximately the same colours as on the website
    scale_fill_continuous(low="white", high="blue", space="rgb") +
    # remove extra space and y breaks
    scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0)) + scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0), breaks=NA)
print(pBar)

# "spiral" version
yMax <- max(d$y)
pBar +
    # switch to polar coord, starting from -pi/2, going anticlockwise
    coord_polar(start=-pi/2, direction=-1) +
    # add extra blank space in the center of the spiral
    scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0), breaks=NA, limits=c(-yMax/5, yMax)) +
    # force the x coordinate (otherwise, NA appear for some reason)
    scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0), limits=c(0,p))

# You can even get some interactivity if you are using RStudio (which is the second best thing that happened to R after ggplot2)

# package the code into a function
ggspiral <- function(x, y, p) {

    # remove period from time coordinate
    xx <- x %% p

    # compute number of periods elapsed
    yy <- floor(x / p)

    # prepare data
    d <- data.frame(xx, yy, y)
    yyMax <- max(yy)

    require("ggplot2")
    ggplot(d) +
        # plot tiles of the appropriate colour
        geom_tile(aes(x=xx, y=yy, fill=y)) +
        # switch to polar coord, starting from -pi/2, going anticlockwise
        coord_polar(start=-pi/2, direction=-1) +
        # add extra blank space in the center of the spiral
        scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0), breaks=NA, limits=c(-yyMax/5, yyMax)) +
        # force the x coordinate (otherwise, NA appear for some reason)
        scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0), limits=c(0,p))
}

library("manipulate")
manipulate(ggspiral(d$day, d$n, p), p=slider(10,50))

I hope this helps.

Jean-Olivier Irisson

d <- read.table("http://www.dartmouth.edu/~chance/teaching_aids/data/birthday.txt", col.names=c("date", "n"))
# create a time coordinate easier to work with
d$day <- seq(from=0, along.with=d$date)
# NB: the plot will only work with a regular time coordinate so if that's not the case, then you should bin the time series beforehand

# Implementation of a true spiral with geom_rect

ggspiral <- function(x, y, p) {

    # remove period from time coordinate
    xx <- x %% p

    dt <- x[2] - x[1]
    xx2 <- xx + dt

    # compute number of periods elapsed

    yy <- x / p
    yy2 <- yy + 1

    # prepare data
    d <- data.frame(xx, xx2, yy, yy2, y)
    yyMax <- max(yy2)

    require("ggplot2")
    ggplot(d) +
        # plot tiles of the appropriate colour

        geom_rect(aes(xmin=xx, xmax=xx2, ymin=yy, ymax=yy2, fill=y)) +

        # switch to polar coord, starting from -pi/2, going anticlockwise
        coord_polar(start=-pi/2, direction=-1) +
        # add extra blank space in the center of the spiral
        scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0), breaks=NA, limits=c(-yyMax/5, yyMax)) +
        # force the x coordinate (otherwise, NA appear for some reason)
        scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0), limits=c(0,p))
}

# in RStudio only

library("manipulate")
manipulate(ggspiral(d$day, d$n, p), p=slider(10,50))

library("reshape")	# for melt
library("ggplot2")

dd<-melt(d,id='theta')	#'wide' format to 'long' format
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=dd, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")

How about as above?
# This 'wide' / 'long' format issue is one of troubles for beginners
such as I.
# e.g.
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/c0ec4b776b28a051/beacc26e4545e0f0?lnk=gst&q=Stacked+Bar+Charts#beacc26e4545e0f0

# Tips
# 1. How to use only a part of variables.
# 1-1. melt with given column names only.
# (use given names during 'wide' to 'long').
d2<-d
d2$vist_per100<-d2$vist/100
d2$pusht_m0_05_x1000<-(d2$pusht - 0.05)*1000
d2$treet_m0_21_x100<-(d2$treet - 0.21)*100

d3<-melt(d2,id='theta',
measure.vars=c('treet_m0_21_x100','vist_per100','pusht_m0_05_x1000'))
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d3, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")

# 1-2. choose rows of given variables and drop unused levels.
# (use given names when already 'wide')
dd<-melt(d,id='theta')
d4<-dd[dd[,'variable'] %in% c('vist','pusht'),]	# choose rows of given
variables
d4[,'variable']<-d4[,'variable'][,drop=TRUE]	# drop unused levels
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d4, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")

# 2. reorder variables.
d3<-melt(d2,id='theta',
measure.vars=c('treet_m0_21_x100','vist_per100','pusht_m0_05_x1000'))
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d3, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")
d3[,2]<-factor(d3[,
2],c('pusht_m0_05_x1000','vist_per100','treet_m0_21_x100'))	#reorder
variables
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d3, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")

# 3. change order of legend separately from plot.
	# from
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/a1eb9d1a57de9ba7/10c682b40a3b865f?lnk=gst&q=coord_flip+legend#10c682b40a3b865f
vars<-c('treet_m0_21_x100','vist_per100','pusht_m0_05_x1000')
d3<-melt(d2,id='theta', measure.vars=vars)
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d3, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")
qplot(factor(theta), value, data=d3, fill=factor(variable), geom =
"bar")+scale_fill_hue(breaks=rev(vars))

>    dataNames<-names(coffs)[!names(coffs) == "levels"]
>    for(i in dataNames) {
>      aess <- aes_string(y=i)
>      aess["colour"] <- i
>      last_plot() + geom_line(aess)

>

This is what I told you above: you need to " create a new column in the dataset with the cut version of hwy"

library("ggplot2")

# for information
head(mpg)

# cut hwy in factor levels

class(mpg$hwyF)

qplot(x=hwyF, fill=class, data=mpg, geom="histogram")
# or
ggplot() + geom_histogram(aes(x=hwyF, fill=class), data=mpg)

messages.subject: ggplot2 plot layout diagram? [SEC=UNCLASSIFIED]
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

As a newcomer to "ggplot2" I find myself at odds with
    trying to imagine what the various parts of a plot
    are called in terms of "ggplot2".

In the book "The LaTeX Companion",
    by Goosens, Mittelbach and Samarin,
    Addison-Wesley Co. Inc., 1994,
    there is a page layout diagram which shows
    the body, the header, the footer, and
    margin notes areas, and has pointers to
    various LaTeX commands that control
    these various elements of page layout.

Does anyone know if such a diagram exists for "ggplot2" ?

Perhaps there is something like this in the "ggplot2" book?
    I hope so.  I'll order that later today.

By my way of thinking, such a diagram would immensely
    help users to understand what they need to tweak
    to get "ggplot2" to produce just what they need.

Best regards,

Lawson Hanson
-------------
    CAWCR, Climate Variability and Change group,
    Climate Change Science team,
    Bureau of Meteorology, 700 Collins Street,
    Melbourne Docklands, VIC 3008
    Telephone: +61 3 9669 4763

library('devtools')
dev_mode()     # should reply dev_mode: ON
install_github('ggplot2')
install_github('scales')
library('ggplot2')
library('scales')
<your code here>

access and use the new version.

    plot (See the example in attached PDF file "z-wv-c.pdf").

    so that the X-axis is -90., through 0., through +90.,
    with no extra graph plot area on each side.

    would be really appreciated.

The 'R' code used to produce the attached plot is:

    library(ggplot2)
    #
    # WvTr <- read.table("Wv-tr.dat", header=T)

messages.subject: Re: Plot a raster layer from raster package with the new geom_raster
messages.subject_clean: Plot a raster layer from raster package with the new geom_raster
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

The help page of geom_raster() in 0.9.0 starts out with the following:

"This is a special case of geom_tile where all tiles are the same
size. It is implemented highly efficiently using the internal
rasterGrob function."

Implicit in this statement is that the input data to the geom is a
data frame. From what little I know about the raster package, it
generates its own classes of objects, so it's possible that you need
to convert objects from the raster package into a different format
that ggplot2 will accept.

You might find the rasterVis package useful; by poking around a
little, I discovered a function gplot() which appears to prepare data
objects from the raster package for use in a subsequent ggplot() call.
See the examples section of its help page for a couple of
illustrations.  Another possibility is the ggmap package developed by
David Kahle, which has more options for adding maps as background
layers in a ggplot. Like ggplot2, ggmap is in active development.

If you want to plot a raster image in a ggplot, look into
annotation_raster() or annotation_custom(). Section 4 of the
transition guide shows a couple of examples where images were added to
a graph or used as the plot background. The term 'raster' gets bandied
about a bit loosely these days so I'm easily confused about what the
term means.

When you get a solution, would you be kind enough to share it here?
There are several people on this list who have a strong interest in
using ggplot2 for spatial maps. I have a couple of examples in the
sections on geom_map() and geom_raster() in the transition guide, with
a few more in geom_polygon(), but I'm fully aware that's not even
scratching the surface of the potential applications of ggplot2 with
spatial data.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: display subset of a data frame
messages.subject_clean: display subset of a data frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Use the subset() function; e.g.,

ggplot(subset(mydata, kind == 1), aes(...)) + ...

You might also consider faceting (a.k.a. conditioning) by kind;
facet_grid() contains arguments to allow free scales in the x
direction, the y direction or both; free scales in one dimension is in
the development version 0.9.0 but not in 0.8.9. The help page of
facet_grid() in 0.9.0 contains a lot of useful examples.

Dennis

> Hi Manuel:
>
> The help page of geom_raster() in 0.9.0 starts out with the following:
>
> "This is a special case of geom_tile where all tiles are the same
> size. It is implemented highly efficiently using the internal
> rasterGrob function."
>
> Implicit in this statement is that the input data to the geom is a

> to convert objects from the raster package into a different format
> that ggplot2 will accept.

> transition guide shows a couple of examples where images were added to

messages.body_plain:
So for the premature send earlier.
==========================
Hello ggplot community,

I'm using ggplot for creating chloropleths and have the need to plot county names on a state map.  Most names plot beautifully but a few need tweaking.  Tweaking could be made much easier with a locator for ggplot while working with maps.  I put forth this problem at stackoverflow.com <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9450873/locator-equivalent-in-ggplot2-for-maps> and received terrific assistance in solving the problem.  Dwin and Baptise worked together to give me the items to build a function for locator capabilities on a map in ggplot.  It still feels like there's something better as it currently only works with one click at a time.  Is there a better way to approach this problem (maybe even something more universal that works outside of maps) or is this it?

Here is a link to the locator code in my drop box as well: http://dl.dropbox.com/u/61803503/gglocator.txt

Thank you in advance.

Hi Tyler -

Nice function!

It didn't work when I copied/pasted directly into R (and I didn't check to see why), but I did some editing and got this perhaps more useful version :

ggmap_loc <- function(object = last_plot(), message = FALSE, xexpand = c(.05,0), yexpand = c(.05, 0)){
  x <- grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(print = message)[[1]]
  x <- x[ grep("panel-", grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(print=message)[[1]]) ] #locate the panel
  seekViewport(x)
  loc <-  as.numeric(grid.locator("npc"))

  xrng <- with(object, range(data[,deparse(mapping$x)]))
  yrng <- with(object, range(data[,deparse(mapping$y)]))

  xrng <- expand_range(range = xrng, mul = xexpand[1], add = xexpand[2])
  yrng <- expand_range(range = yrng, mul = yexpand[1], add = yexpand[2])

  c(xrng[1] + loc[1]*diff(xrng), yrng[1] + loc[2]*diff(yrng))
}

# df <- data.frame(xvar = 2:10, yvar = 2:10)
# qplot(xvar, yvar, data = df) + annotate(geom = 'point', x = 3, y = 6)
# ggmap_loc()

I'm sure there is  a more efficient way to do this (i.e. pulling from the object scales directly without having to recalculate them), but this works fine.  It can also apply to any ggplot as you see in the minimal example underneath.

Neat!

david.

And actually coming across a use for it in something I am doing (good timing!), this is even better.  Better name, too.

gglocator <- function(n = 1, object = last_plot(), message = FALSE, xexpand = c(.05,0), yexpand = c(.05, 0)){

  if(n > 1){
    df <- NULL
    for(k in 1:n){
      df <- rbind(df, gglocator(object = object, message = message,
        xexpand = xexpand, yexpand = yexpand))
    }
    return(df)

  }

  x <- grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(print = message)[[1]]

  x <- x[ grep("panel-", grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(print=message)[[1]]) ] #locate the panel
  seekViewport(x)

  loc <-  as.numeric(grid.locator("npc"))

  xrng <- with(object, range(data[,deparse(mapping$x)]))
  yrng <- with(object, range(data[,deparse(mapping$y)]))

  xrng <- expand_range(range = xrng, mul = xexpand[1], add = xexpand[2])
  yrng <- expand_range(range = yrng, mul = yexpand[1], add = yexpand[2])

  point <- data.frame(xrng[1] + loc[1]*diff(xrng), yrng[1] + loc[2]*diff(yrng))
  names(point) <- with(object, c(deparse(mapping$x), deparse(mapping$y)))
  point
}

messages.subject: Re: dotsize behavior in geom_dotplot
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Feb 27, 2012 at 6:15 PM, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Tom -
>
> The diameter is determined by the binwidth value  -- the diameter (when dotsize=1) is the same as the binwidth. The value of dotsize tells it to scale relative to binwidth. At present there's no way to set the dot size to be an absolute size. That wouldn't be too hard to do, though. When I wrote the code, it didn't occur to me that people might want to use dot plots this way, but I can see how it might be useful.
>

The change to allow absolute dot sizes was pretty simple. There's now a parameter called abs_size. You can install the modified version and run this example:

library(devtools)
dev_mode()
install_github('ggplot2', 'wch', 'experimental')
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", aes(x = 50), method = "histodot",
               dotsize = 2, binwidth = 2, abs_size = TRUE) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "x", aes(y = 80), method = "histodot",

               dotsize = 2, binwidth = 10, abs_size = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +

  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

The stuff with the scales removes the padding, so that the dot stacks go right on the edge.

Bear in mind that the dot diameter now has no relation to the bin width. I used histodot binning because using dot-density binning would be more confusing in this case, where the dot diameter doesn't tell you anything about bin width. Still, even histodot binning could be misleading if the dot diameter is wildly different from bin width.

-Winston

Slight correction: the baseline of the vertical dot stacks will be at y=0, unless you set it like this:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", aes(x = 20), method = "histodot",
               dotsize = 2, binwidth = 2, abs_size = TRUE) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "x", y = 5, method = "histodot",
               dotsize = 2, binwidth = 10, abs_size = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits=c(5, 35))

Notice that it's different from how x works -- the x position has to be set inside the aes(). There are some technical reasons for this... basically, it boils down to the the fact that x and y are treated somewhat differently in ggplot, and this geom wasn't designed for marginal plots like this.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: dotsize behavior in geom_dotplot
messages.body_plain:
I think I have a better solution... It doesn't require an absolute dot size, so it can be run with the regular version of ggplot2. It does, however, require you to specify the ratio of width to height of your output graphic. It also needs you to specify x and y range, but if you're clever about it, you can calculate it using range() and then expanding a bit to give room for the marginal dot plots.

The advantage to this code is that the dot width is always meaningful -- in the previous example I gave with dot size specified in mm, the dot width had no determinate relation to the bin width, and so you could have bins that are much narrower or wider than the dots. Adding to the confusion is that the relation can be different on the two axes: the bins could be narrower than the dots on one axis, and wider than the dots on the other.

xyratio <- 2/1     # Ratio of width/height in output graphic

xrange <- c(20,500)
yrange <- c(5,35)

nxbins <- 60       # Number of bins on x-axis
nybins <- nxbins / xyratio

xbinwidth <- diff(xrange)/nxbins
ybinwidth <- diff(yrange)/nybins

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +

  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", aes(x = xrange[1]), binwidth = ybinwidth) +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "x", y = yrange[1], binwidth = xbinwidth) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = xrange) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = yrange)

I've attached two versions: one where the x:y ratio is 1:1, and another where its 2:1. The x and y dot sizes aren't exactly the same in the 2:1 version, because even though the overall image is a perfect 2:1 ratio (400x200), the plotting area isn't exactly 2:1. Tweaking the value of xyratio would fix this.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Geometric resolution of large-n polar plot
messages.subject_clean: Geometric resolution of large-n polar plot
messages.body_plain:
The issue is with the ggplot2:::coord_munch function, which has an argument segment_length with a default value of .01:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/R/coord-munch.r

I don't think there's any place to pass in arguments that will make it down to coord_munch's segment_length argument. One way to deal with it for now is to replace the coord_munch function with a duplicate that has a different default value for segment_length.

# Save the original version of coord_munch
coord_munch_old <- ggplot2:::coord_munch

# Make a wrapper function that has a different default for segment_length
coord_munch_new <- function(coord, data, range, segment_length = 1/500) {
  coord_munch_old(coord, data, range, segment_length)
}
# Make the new function run in the same environment
environment(coord_munch_new) <- environment(ggplot2:::coord_munch)

# Replace ggplot2:::coord_munch with coord_munch_new
assignInNamespace("coord_munch", coord_munch_new, ns="ggplot2")

# Run the example
set.seed(123)
df <- data.frame(
  x = sort(sample(1:40, 400, replace=TRUE)),
  y = sample(0:9, 400, replace=TRUE)
)

pdf('polar.pdf')
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=y)) +
  geom_bar(stat='identity', position="fill") +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="blue", high="pink")
dev.off()

Assigning values in a namespace is only supposed to be used for development purposes, so this is not a good long-term solution. Also, I tested this only with the upcoming version, 0.9.0 -- I don't know if it'll work correctly with 0.8.9.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Geometric resolution of large-n polar plot
messages.subject_clean: Geometric resolution of large-n polar plot
messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Feb-28, at 18:03 , geotheory wrote:
>
> I have an issue with a large polar plot - because of how coord_polar
> works the central rings have very low polygonal resolution and are way
> too jagged.  I've illustrated this in stackoverflow (please ignore the
> misclassification by admins of it as a PDF output issue).
>
> http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9483033/increase-resolution-of-ggplot-when-saving-to-pdf
>
> Grateful for assistance!

This is because bars in cardinal coordinates are "bent" into the polar coordinate space through what is called "munching" in ggplot. Munching means basically cutting the original shape into small bits and recomputing the coordinates of those bits in the new (polar) space, hence getting a nice polygon. How small the bits are determines how good the final polygon is looking. This is controlled by segment_length in the function coord_much of coord_munch.r in ggplot's source. Unfortunately, this is not user visible.

I, personally, would like to have this visible if you can find a way.

Beyond this, I was surprised because, from what I understand from the code, segment_length is expressed in terms of physical distance on the plot, scaled between 0 and 1. So increasing the bar physical dimensions by moving them away from the center should get them munched. But it doesn't:

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
df <- data.frame(
  x = sort(sample(1:40, 400, replace=TRUE)),
  y = sample(0:9, 400, replace=TRUE)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=y)) +

  geom_bar(stat='identity', position="fill") +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="blue", high="pink")

Instead, changing the data to increase the coordinate values in the data space, by doing something like this:

ggplot(df, aes(x=x+100, y=y, fill=y)) +

  geom_bar(stat='identity', position="fill") +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="blue", high="pink")

does get them munched. Doing this computation in the data space seems odd because everything should be rescaled to [0,1] anyway. And indeed, as long as the computation is proportional (multiplication, division, etc.) the results are exactly the same:

ggplot(df, aes(x=x*100, y=y, fill=y)) +

  geom_bar(stat='identity', position="fill") +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="blue", high="pink")

ggplot(df, aes(x=x/100, y=y, fill=y)) +

  geom_bar(stat='identity', position="fill") +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="blue", high="pink")

Maybe there is a bug lurking.

would be the corresponding pattern of the second variable. The idea is

density estimation. Now I need to bin the first variable accordingly
and map them to a categorical value.

Is there R command that can do this?

Robert
